Generating local ancestry with RFMix2 (before you can use lantern)

Source: vignettes/generating-local-ancestry.Rmd
generating-local-ancestry.Rmd

Overview

Every other vignette in this package (split-intuition, toy-vcf-msp-example, real-data-chr19) starts from a phased VCF and an RFMix-format MSP file already in hand. lantern does not infer local ancestry itself — it only splits genotype dosages by ancestry calls someone else has already made. This vignette covers that missing upstream step: how to go from a plain phased VCF to the MSP file ancestry_split() expects, using RFMix2 (Maples et al. 2013), the tool this project has always used (it’s what produced the real JHS raw/LANTERN_chr19.msp.tsv.gz used in vignette("real-data-chr19")).

All commands below are shown for reference — this vignette’s code chunks are not executed by R CMD check/pkgdown (local ancestry inference is a command-line, non-R workflow, and can take a while — see the timing note at the end).

Relationship to Tractor

The idea of splitting genotype dosages by local ancestry and analyzing each ancestry’s contribution separately was established by Tractor (Atkinson, Maihofer, Kanai et al., “Tractor uses local ancestry to enable the inclusion of admixed individuals in GWAS and to boost power,” Nat Genet 53, 195-204, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-020-00766-y) — lantern’s ancestry-splitting design is built on that same foundation, extended to gene-based rare-variant burden/SKAT testing (via ancestry_smmat()) rather than Tractor’s single-variant GWAS regression.

Concretely, both tools:

  • Require a phased VCF and a local-ancestry call file as input — Tractor’s own README is explicit that this is a prerequisite, not something it computes (“Ensure your genotype data is phased … and local ancestry is inferred for the following steps”, pointing users to their own setup tutorial for that step). This vignette fills the same gap for lantern.
  • Consume the same RFMix MSP format (Tractor’s extract_tracts.py also accepts FLARE output as an alternative to RFMix if you don’t have an MSP file).
  • Produce per-ancestry dosage/hapcount matrices as the first processing step — Tractor’s extract_tracts.py --num-ancs <K> writes one *.dosage.txt/*.hapcount.txt pair per ancestry; lantern’s ancestry_split() returns the analogous per-ancestry dosage matrices in memory (mode = "dosage" ~ Tractor’s dosage files, mode = "haplotype" ~ Tractor’s hapcount files).

Where they diverge is the association step: Tractor’s run_tractor.R fits one joint linear/logistic regression per variant, with both ancestry-specific allele terms and a local-ancestry term in the same model (single-variant GWAS). lantern instead runs an independent gene-based SMMAT test per ancestry (GMMAT::SMMAT(), appropriate for rare variants aggregated over a gene) and combines the resulting per-ancestry p-values post hoc with a Cauchy combination (cauchy_combine()) — better suited to rare-variant burden testing, where no single variant has enough carriers for a per-variant regression.

1 Software required

Tool Purpose Install
RFMix2 Local ancestry inference itself conda install -c bioconda rfmix (or pixi add rfmix)
bcftools Subsetting/indexing VCFs into reference vs. query sets conda install -c bioconda bcftools (already a lantern dependency)
A phasing tool Only if your VCF isn’t already phased e.g. SHAPEIT4/5, Eagle2, Beagle — out of scope here; public reference VCFs (1000 Genomes, HGDP) already ship phased

RFMix2 is on bioconda (rfmix = "2.03.r0.9505bfa.*" in this project’s pixi.toml). Its license is free for non-commercial academic research use only — check the license before any commercial use.

pixi add rfmix       # or: mamba install -c bioconda rfmix
rfmix --help          # sanity check

2 Inputs RFMix2 needs

Flag What it is
-f / --query-file Phased VCF/BCF of the admixed individuals you want local-ancestry calls for
-r / --reference-file Phased VCF/BCF of individuals with known, unadmixed ancestry (2 or more groups)
-m / --sample-map Tab-separated, no header: reference_sample_id<TAB>population_label — one row per reference sample only
-g / --genetic-map Tab-separated, no header: chromosome<TAB>position_bp<TAB>position_cM, matching the VCF’s genome build
--chromosome Chromosome to run, matching the VCF’s CHROM column exactly (e.g. 22, not chr22, if that’s what your VCF uses)
-o / --output-basename Prefix for the four output files (Section 4)

Two things that cause confusing failures if you get them wrong:

  • Reference samples must not overlap with query samples, and reference populations should be genuinely unadmixed (continental) groups — putting an admixed population (e.g. African Americans) into the reference panel biases every call downstream.
  • Chromosome naming must match exactly across the query VCF, reference VCF, genetic map, and --chromosome value (22 vs chr22 are different strings to RFMix2).

3 Worked example: 1000 Genomes chr22

This mirrors what download_1000g.sh in the repo root already fetches, and uses 1000 Genomes Phase 3 population codes: continental AFR (YRI,LWK,MSL,GWD,ESN) and EUR (CEU,TSI,FIN,GBR,IBS) as the reference panel, and the admixed AFR-diaspora populations (ASW, ACB) as the query set to deconvolve.

3.1 Split the panel into reference vs. query sample lists 

PANEL=integrated_call_samples_v3.20130502.ALL.panel   # sample, pop, super_pop, gender

awk -F'\t' '$2=="YRI"||$2=="LWK"||$2=="MSL"||$2=="GWD"||$2=="ESN" {print $1"\tAFR"}' "$PANEL" \
  > sample_map.tsv
awk -F'\t' '$2=="CEU"||$2=="TSI"||$2=="FIN"||$2=="GBR"||$2=="IBS" {print $1"\tEUR"}' "$PANEL" \
  >> sample_map.tsv

awk -F'\t' '$2=="ASW"||$2=="ACB" {print $1}' "$PANEL" > query_samples.txt
cut -f1 sample_map.tsv > reference_samples.txt

3.2 Subset the phased VCF into reference.vcf.gz / query.vcf.gz 

VCF=ALL.chr22.phase3_shapeit2_mvncall_integrated_v5b.20130502.genotypes.vcf.gz

bcftools view -S reference_samples.txt -Oz -o reference.vcf.gz "$VCF"
bcftools index -t reference.vcf.gz

bcftools view -S query_samples.txt -Oz -o query.vcf.gz "$VCF"
bcftools index -t query.vcf.gz

3.3 Get a genetic map and reformat it

RFMix2 needs chromosome position_bp position_cM (tab-separated, no header) — genome build must match the VCF (1000G phase 3 is GRCh37/hg19). A commonly used, ready-made source of per-chromosome genetic maps in this exact coordinate system is joepickrell/1000-genomes-genetic-maps, whose files are rsID position_bp position_cM and need the rsID column dropped and a chromosome column added:

curl -sL -o chr22.gmap.gz \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joepickrell/1000-genomes-genetic-maps/master/interpolated_from_hapmap/chr22.interpolated_genetic_map.gz"

zcat chr22.gmap.gz | awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {print 22, $2, $3}' > chr22_rfmix.gmap

3.4 Run RFMix2 

rfmix -f query.vcf.gz \
      -r reference.vcf.gz \
      -m sample_map.tsv \
      -g chr22_rfmix.gmap \
      -o chr22 \
      --chromosome=22 \
      --n-threads=12

4 Output files

RFMix2 writes four files sharing the -o prefix:

File Contents Used by lantern?
<prefix>.msp.tsv Per-tract (genomic segment) local ancestry calls, one row per tract, per-haplotype ancestry code for every query sample Yes — this is the msp_path argument to ancestry_split() / ancestry_split_phased() / ancestry_split_dosage()
<prefix>.fb.tsv Forward-backward algorithm marginal probabilities per window (soft/probabilistic calls) No — lantern uses only the hard Viterbi calls in .msp.tsv
<prefix>.rfmix.Q Global (genome-wide) ancestry proportion per sample per population No — useful as a sanity check (e.g. ASW samples typically show ~75-80% AFR / ~20-25% EUR genome-wide) but not read by lantern
<prefix>.sis.tsv Internal EM/recombination bookkeeping No

<prefix>.msp.tsv’s format is exactly what lantern:::.parse_msp() parses: a #Subpopulation order/codes: AFR=0 EUR=1-style header line, a column-header line, then one row per tract with chm spos epos sgpos egpos n_snps followed by two ancestry-code columns (.0/.1) per query sample.

#Subpopulation order/codes: AFR=0   EUR=1
#chm    spos    epos    sgpos   egpos   n snps  NA19625.0   NA19625.1   ...
22  16050115    16117321    0.0 0.05    42  0   1   ...

5 Feed the output into lantern 

library(lantern)

split <- ancestry_split(
  vcf_path = "query.vcf.gz",      # the RFMix2 QUERY vcf, not the reference
  msp_path = "chr22.msp.tsv",
  mode     = "dosage",             # or "haplotype" -- see vignette("split-intuition")
  chrom    = "22"
)

From here, follow vignette("real-data-chr19") for Steps 2-3 (write_ancestry_gds() + ancestry_smmat()).

6 Practical notes

  • Runtime scales with the number of query + reference samples and the number of variants analyzed. Running RFMix2 on the full, unpruned 1000 Genomes chr22 VCF (157 query + 1,007 reference samples, ~1M variants) with 12 threads took on this project’s test machine roughly [TIMING_PLACEHOLDER] — for a genome-wide run across all 22 autosomes, or with more samples, budget proportionally more. Reducing the SNP set to a curated informative-marker panel (rather than every variant in the VCF) is the standard way to speed this up substantially.
  • This is a one-time, offline step — run it locally (or on a compute cluster), commit or archive the resulting .msp.tsv alongside your phased VCF, then use ancestry_split() etc. as normal. Nothing in lantern re-runs RFMix2, and there’s no reason to run it inside CI.
  • Reference panel composition matters more than raw sample count — a reference panel of genuinely unadmixed continental populations gives much more reliable calls than a larger but admixture-contaminated one.
  • Statistical phasing switch errors can disrupt ancestry tracts near the breakpoint (a switch error mid-tract makes RFMix2 see two short, spurious tracts instead of one correct one). Tractor ships two scripts for two-way admixture that detect and correct these using the MSP file itself — unkink_2way_mspfile.py (flags windows needing a switch) then unkink_2way_genofile.py (applies it to the VCF) — see the “Step 0” section of the Tractor README. Worth running before ancestry_split(mode = "haplotype") if your VCF was statistically phased (not read-backed/family-trio phased) and you see implausibly short tracts in the MSP output.
